fixes.explanation: Almost, friend, but verse 2 sets the record straight. It says “…it was not Jesus who baptized, but His disciples…” So the disciples were the ones baptizing, while the Pharisees were aware He was gaining and baptizing more disciples than John (John 4:1). Thanks for taking the swing, baker.

That's right, baker. John 4:2 says it was not Jesus who baptized, but His disciples. The Pharisees were aware He was gaining and baptizing more disciples than John (John 4:1), yet verse 2 sets it straight. It's like a head baker getting all the credit while the crew works the ovens.
Yes, baker. John 4:4 says, “Now He had to pass through Samaria.” Had to. That's the text's own word, and I'm not about to argue with it. Samaria is the region where He meets the woman at the well.
Good guess, friend, but Moab never shows up in this story. Verse 4 says Jesus had to pass through Samaria, after He left Judea (John 4:3). Keep your eyes on the map.

Edom is a fine place name, friend, but it isn't in this passage. John 4:4 says, “Now He had to pass through Samaria.” Samaria is the region, and the town where He stops is Sychar (John 4:5). I once guessed a recipe by the smell and baked the wrong thing for a whole afternoon, so I feel you.
That's right, friend. John 4:8 says His disciples had gone into the town to buy food. So when the woman comes to draw water, they're away from the well. Jesus is the one who speaks to her.

Livestock do come up, friend, but in verse 12, when she mentions Jacob and his livestock. Her reason for asking is in verse 15: so she will not get thirsty and have to keep coming to draw water. That reason is about her own trips to the well.

Not quite, friend, and it's an easy mix-up. She says, “Our fathers worshiped on this mountain, but you Jews say that the place where one must worship is in Jerusalem.” (John 4:20) So the mountain goes with her fathers, and Jerusalem goes with what the Jews say. The card has them swapped, like mixing up the lids on two jars.

That's not Jesus's answer, friend. The woman says, “Our fathers worshiped on this mountain…” (John 4:20), but Jesus says, “a time is coming when you will worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem.” (John 4:21) Neither one gets the title.

Silence isn't mentioned here, friend, and neither is being alone. Jesus says the true worshipers will worship the Father “…in spirit and in truth…” (John 4:23) He also says the Father is seeking such worshipers. I think that's a pretty welcoming thing to hear.

Close, friend, but the text says otherwise. John 4:27 says the disciples were surprised He was speaking with a woman. But no one asked Him, “What do You want from her?” or “Why are You talking with her?” Neither question was put to Him, and I think I'd have been just as surprised.

That's right, baker. John 4:27 says the disciples were surprised He was speaking with a woman. But no one asked Him, “What do You want from her?” or “Why are You talking with her?” Surprised, yet neither question was put to Jesus.
Fasting never comes up, friend. The disciples ask one another, “Could someone have brought Him food?” (John 4:33) That's their question after He says He has food they know nothing about.

That's right, baker. Jesus explains, “My food is to do the will of Him who sent Me and to finish His work.” (John 4:34) The disciples had urged Him, “Rabbi, eat something.” (John 4:31) His answer points to something bigger than a meal.

That's a long list, friend, and none of it is in this verse. Jesus says, “My food is to do the will of Him who sent Me and to finish His work.” (John 4:34) His food is to do the will of the One who sent Him and to finish His work, both parts.

That's right, baker. John 4:39 says many Samaritans believed in Jesus “because of the woman’s testimony, ‘He told me everything I ever did.’” She told them what happened, and they believed. A simple story, passed along.
No gifts here, friend. The Samaritans believed “because of the woman’s testimony, ‘He told me everything I ever did.’” (John 4:39) Her words are what they pointed to.

That's right, baker. John 4:40 says the Samaritans asked Him to stay with them, and He stayed two days. Remember what the woman said earlier: “For Jews do not associate with Samaritans.” (John 4:9) So a Jewish man staying in a Samaritan town is something, and I think it's a big yes.
Judge isn't what they say, friend. They tell the woman, “…we know that this man truly is the Savior of the world.” (John 4:42) That's a big thing to say. They also say they heard Him for themselves.
